bib.title: CCNet: Extracting High Quality Monolingual Datasets from Web Crawl Data

legacy_report:
SOURCE: CCNet: Extracting High Quality Monolingual Datasets from Web Crawl Data. Guillaume Wenzek, Marie-Anne Lachaux (equal contribution), Alexis Conneau, Vishrav Chaudhary, Francisco Guzmán, Armand Joulin, Edouard Grave (Facebook AI). arXiv 1911.00359v2, 15 Nov 2019. The extracted text gives no venue; the LREC 2020 label comes from your brief, not from the PDF.

COVERAGE: I read all 33,472 of 33,472 chars across 6 pages: body, references, and the per-language Table 3 appendix (I skimmed the table rows and pulled out the key languages). Nothing was skipped.

PIPELINE (Sec. 3, Fig. 1). Runs on each monthly snapshot of WET (UTF-8 text) files:
1. Shard WET files into 5GB JSON shards, about 1600 for Feb 2019.
2. Normalise each paragraph: lowercase, digits to 0, strip Unicode punctuation and accents. Hash each paragraph with the first 64 bits of SHA-1 and save the hashes to binary files.
3. Remove duplicate paragraphs by comparing a shard against 1 shard, a subset of shards, or all of them.
4. Run fastText language ID and keep a page only if its top-language score is above 0.5. This runs after dedup, which reverses Grave et al. 2018's order.
5. Tokenise with SentencePiece, then score with a 5-gram Kneser-Ney KenLM model trained on Wikipedia in that language (48 languages).
6. Split each language into head/middle/tail terciles by perplexity, with thresholds set per language.
Nothing is removed on LM score. The buckets are labels only.

CLAIMS
- claim: Duplicate paragraphs make up most of the text in a snapshot.
  number: 70%
  setup: duplicates across web pages within one snapshot
  quote: "removing dupli-cated paragraphs across the different web pages in a snap-shot, as they represent 70% of the text"
  where: p2, Sec 3.2
- claim: How much survives dedup depends on how many shards' hashes you compare against.
  number: 42% remaining (1 shard), 28% (100 shards)
  setup: one shard of Feb 2019, share of characters remaining
  quote: "After deduplication across 1 shard, there is 42% of characters remaining and 28% across 100 shards."
  where: p3, Sec 4.2
- claim: Comparing against 50 shards was chosen as the RAM/recall trade-off.
  number: 1.5B hashes, 13.5GB disk, 40GB RAM, 3% of corpus
  setup: memory-efficient hashset (parallel-hashmap)
  quote: "Loading hashes from 50 represents 1.5B unique hashes, making up 13.5GB on disk. Using a memory efﬁcient hash-set3 we can ﬁt those into 40GB of RAM." / "We found 50 shards to be a reasonable trade-off and are therefore running the deduplication on blocks corresponding to 3% of the corpus."
  where: p3, Sec 4.2
- claim: BERT trained on head-tercile CommonCrawl beats the same model trained on Wikipedia on XNLI, by 3.3 points on average.
  number: avg 72.6 (Wiki) vs 75.9 (CC); en 82.8/85.0, ru 73.3/76.4, zh 77.0/77.9, ur 57.3/64.3
  setup: BERT-BASE without NSP; Wiki corpora of 16G/5G/1.1G/106M against head CC capped at 21G/21G/17G/2.2G for en/ru/zh/ur; every model early-stopped after 2 days on 16 Volta32 GPUs with the same step count; XNLI dev, trained on each language's own training data
  quote: "BERT-BASE models trained on CommonCrawl outperform identical models trained on Wikipedia by 3.3% on average." Table 2: "Wiki 82.8 73.3 77.0 57.3 72.6 / CC 85.0 76.4 77.9 64.3 75.9"
  where: p5, Sec 5.3, Table 2
- claim: For Urdu, a Wikipedia-pretrained BERT does about as well as a random init, and CCNet data adds 7 points.
  number: 7 points
  setup: ur, 106M of Wikipedia vs 2.2G of CC head
  quote: "the model pretrained on Wikipedia obtains similar performance than a randomly initialized model. Using our corpus in-stead, we obtain a 7 points improvement in accuracy"
  where: p5, Sec 5.3
- claim: fastText embeddings get steadily better from tail to head, which supports perplexity as a quality signal.
  number: English total 62.0 tail / 74.2 mid / 77.9 head; Polish 59.9 / 62.8 / 65.3
  setup: 300-dim fastText trained on each tercile, scored on Mikolov 2013 semantic/syntactic analogies
  quote: "head 77.9 81.2 75.3 65.3 66.5 64.1 / mid. 74.2 79.0 70.4 62.8 62.7 63.0 / tail 62.0 68.1 57.3 59.9 59.8 60.1"
  where: p5, Table 1
- claim: One Feb 2019 snapshot yields 1.5B documents in 174 languages. English is 532B tokens, 120 times BERT's data.
  number: 1.5B docs, 174 languages, 700M English docs, 532B tokens, 120x
  setup: Feb 2019 snapshot
  quote: "the dataset obtained by pre-processing the February 2019 snapshot is composed of 1.5 billions documents in 174 lan-guages. There are 700 millions ﬁltered documents in En-glish alone, corresponding to 532 billions tokens. That is 120 times bigger than the data used in Devlin et al. (2018)."
  where: p1, Intro
- claim: Output sizes by language.
  number: 3.2TB compressed; en 532B tokens / 706M docs; ru 101B / 167M; zh 92B; de 105M docs; 11 languages >10B tokens; 27 >1B
  setup: Feb 2019, after the pipeline; tokens counted with the pipeline's SentencePiece
  quote: "we get 3.2TB of compressed docu-ments in 174 languages" / "The three largest languages are English (en) with 532B to-kens, Russian (ru) with 101B tokens and Chinese (zh) with 92B tokens. We obtained 11 languages with more than 10B tokens, and 27 languages with more than 1B tokens."
  where: p4, Sec 5.1
- claim: For some low-resource languages, one snapshot holds more text than Wikipedia does.
  number: af/gu/km/my 160/190/154/440MB vs Wikipedia 103/88/71/153MB
  setup: Feb 2019 snapshot
  quote: "Afrikaans (af), Gujarati (gu), Khmer (km) and Burmese (my) contains re-spectively 160MB, 190MB, 154MB and 440MB of data. In comparison Wikipedia contains 103MB, 88MB, 71MB and 153MB of data for these languages."
  where: p4, Sec 5.1
- claim: Input scale per snapshot.
  number: 20–30TB, about 3B pages; Feb 2019 = 24TB, 1600 shards
  quote: "Each snapshot contain between 20 and 30TB of uncom-pressed plain text, corresponding to approximately 3 billion web pages (for instance the Feb. 2019 snapshot contains 24TB of data)."
  where: p2, Sec 3.1
- claim: Compute per snapshot.
  number: 8.5 h on 5000 cores (intro); "about 9 hours" (Sec 4.3); hashing 45 min on 1600 CPUs; 40 min per shard with 17 processes
  quote: "takes 8.5 hours to process per snapshot on 5000 CPU cores" / "The total processing time is about 9 hours using 5000 CPU cores for one snapshot."
  where: p1; p4 Sec 4.3
- claim: How CPU time splits in the second pass.
  number: dedup 40% of time; LID 12.5%; SentencePiece 33%; LM 13%
  quote: "Removing the du-plicated parapgraphs takes 40% of the time." / "The language identiﬁer takes 12.5% of CPU time, sentence piece 33% and the LM 13%."
  where: p4, Sec 4.3
- claim: The fastText language ID covers 176 languages, uses a 0.5 threshold, and runs at 1k documents per second per core.
  number: 176, 0.5, 1k doc/s
  quote: "It supports 176 languages and outputs a score for each of them in the [0, 1] range. It processes 1k documents per second on a sin-gle CPU core." / "If this score is higher than 0.5, we classify the document in the corresponding language."
  where: p2, Sec 3.3
- claim: Running dedup before language ID recovers low-resource documents that boilerplate had pushed into English or into "unidentified". The effect is shown only as a plot (Fig 3, ratios up to about 5x), estimated on 1% of the snapshot.
  number: "1% of Feb. 2019 snapshot"
  quote: "Low resources languages beneﬁts the more from doing ”Deduplication then LID” Stats estimated on 1% of Feb. 2019 snapshot."
  where: p4, Fig 3 caption
- claim: The Wikipedia LMs differ hugely in training size, which is why thresholds are set per language.
  number: en 534M, gu 12M
  quote: "En-glish LM was trained on 534M of text while Gujarati was trained on only 12M."
  where: p5, Sec 5.2

LIMITS:
- Perplexity against Wikipedia rewards text that reads like Wikipedia. The authors concede: "Some documents despite be-ing valid text ends up in the tail because they have a vocabulary very different from Wikipedia. This includes blog comments with spoken-like text, or very specialized forums with speciﬁc jargon." (p5). That is why they keep the tail rather than dropping it. They call perplexity only "a relative good proxy for quality."
- Perplexity distributions differ by language, which they attribute to differences in Wikipedia size, not to how much quality text each language has. This is a postulate, not something they test.
- The downstream results are thin:
  - Each XNLI number is a single run. No seeds, variance or significance are reported.
  - Wiki and CC data volumes are not matched, except roughly for English (16G vs 21G). The ru/zh/ur gains mix data quantity with data quality.
  - Only the head tercile is compared against Wikipedia. There is no BERT run on unfiltered or tail CC data, so the BERT result does not isolate the LM filter. Only the fastText Table 1 compares terciles.
  - No XLM was trained. XLM appears only as a motivation in the Conclusion.
- The dedup study is on one shard. The low-resource LID gain is estimated on 1% of a snapshot, and the authors say LID recall for low-resource languages is weak.
- Inconsistencies in the paper:
  - Total time is 8.5 h in the intro but about 9 h in Sec 4.3.
  - The intro calls the 700M English documents "filtered", but Table 3 counts all documents after dedup across all buckets.
  - The text points to "table 6", but the table is labelled Table 3.
- Dated: the work is from 2019, uses a single Feb 2019 snapshot, and evaluates with BERT-BASE and XNLI only. It is concurrent with T5/C4 (Raffel et al. 2019), which it cites but does not compare against.

BUILDS ON (as printed):
- Grave et al. (2018): the fastText Common Crawl pipeline. CCNet follows it but changes the order to dedup before LID and keeps document structure.
- Mikolov et al. (2017), fastText.
- Joulin et al. (2016a, 2016b): the fastText classifier and language ID.
- Heafield (2011), KenLM.
- Kudo (2018), SentencePiece.
- Ortiz Suárez et al. (2019): an improved Grave pipeline (OSCAR-like).
- Buck et al. (2014): n-gram statistics from Common Crawl.
- Baevski et al. (2019): BERT-like pretraining on CC.
- Lample and Conneau (2019): BERT without NSP, and XLM.
- Raffel et al. (2019): concurrent CC-based dataset. The paper contrasts it with "English speciﬁc preprocessing, such as keeping URLs shared on Reddit or using hand-crafted ﬁltering rules."
- Conneau et al. (2018), XNLI.

CODE: none in the paper. The pipeline, the 48 Wikipedia SentencePiece+KenLM models, and a URL-list reconstruction tool are released at "github.com/facebookresearch/cc_net" (p2, footnote 2).

FIGURES:
- Fig 1 (p2), pipeline diagram ("compute the paragraph hashes ... deduplicate ... language identiﬁcation and compute language model perplexity score ... regroup ... by language and perplexity score"). It shows the two-pass structure (hash first, then filter) at a glance.
- Fig 4 (p4), "Amount of data remaining after deduplication with different fraction of the dataset." One curve shows dedup recall rising with the number of hashes loaded.
- Fig 7 (p6), "Histogram of language model perplexities ... English ... and Gujarati ... Vertical lines correspond to perplexity thresholds applied to split the corpus in head/middle/tail." This makes the per-language tercile thresholds concrete.
- Fig 3 (p4), dedup→LID vs LID→dedup document ratio by language size. It is useful for the order-of-operations point.

PROBLEMS:
- Extraction was clean: no scanned pages and no embedded instructions.
- Line-break hyphens remain in quotes (e.g. "dupli-cated"), and ligatures render as "ﬁ".
- Several captions are cut off in the figures.py output, but the full captions were present in the text extraction.
- Fig 3/4/5 values exist only as plotted axes, so I quote only the numbers stated in the text.
